name: incremental-acceptance-targets
body:
The design is validated against a single reference workload, ~/jgrapht (the fast CI baseline). ~/netbeans is no longer an acceptance workload: by human directive the netbeans smoke test is dropped and the acceptance scenarios are re-scoped onto jgrapht. netbeans (an hour-plus full scan) remains at most motivation for why the optimisation exists — it is never a target that is measured.

Recorded jgrapht full-scan baseline: ~16s wall (12s logged) — Java frontend ~9s (~70%), graph assembly ~1s, DB load ~2s, startup/overhead 3–4s; 21,334 nodes, 153k edges, 18 MB DB. Every acceptance bound below is stated relative to THIS baseline. The retired netbeans-scaled bounds ("single-digit minutes", "~1h+ full scan") are meaningless on jgrapht (~16s full scan) and are not carried over.

Acceptance shape — three scenarios, all on jgrapht:
(1) a fresh worktree is near-instant;
(2) a small (1–5 file) localized edit re-scans incrementally and finishes materially below the recorded jgrapht full-scan baseline. The bound is a stated TARGET, not a measurement: at most half the recorded ~16s wall (~8s), with the Java-frontend phase materially below the recorded ~9s Java-frontend baseline — or reported as `frontend-skipped` on full cache reuse;
(3) a signature change to a widely-depended-on symbol may legitimately approach a full scan, but must stay exact: the incremental graph equals a from-scratch full scan of the same changed tree (same node set, same edge set, same unresolved targets).

AC: the three scenarios are exercised on jgrapht and measured with the per-phase timing report (frontend / ingest-assembly / DB-load / startup-overhead) against the recorded ~16s and ~9s baselines above. No acceptance bound is expressed in netbeans units.
